```{r}
#| label: lectures-10-to-12-code
#| include: false
# The data and functions of lectures 10 to 12
osap_url <- paste0(
  "https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/resolve/",
  "Data-Release-2026.10/Portfolios/Full%20Sets%20OP/PredictorLSretWide.parquet"
)
osap_file <- "data/osap_long_short_returns.parquet"
if (!file.exists(osap_file)) {
  download.file(osap_url, osap_file, mode = "wb")
}
anomalies <- read_parquet(osap_file) |>
  mutate(date = floor_date(as.Date(date), "month")) |>
  filter(between(date, sample_start, sample_end)) |>
  select(date, where(\(x) !anyNA(x)))
returns <- as.matrix(select(anomalies, -date)) / 100
estimation <- anomalies$date < test_start
x_estimation <- returns[estimation, ]

sharpe_ratio <- function(x) mean(x) / sd(x) * sqrt(months_per_year)
ridge_weights <- function(x, lambda) {
  solve(crossprod(x) + nrow(x) * lambda * diag(ncol(x)), colSums(x))
}
folds <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(x_estimation)) / (nrow(x_estimation) / n_folds))
cv_sharpe <- function(fit_weights, lambda) {
  map_dbl(seq_len(n_folds), \(k) {
    weights <- fit_weights(x_estimation[folds != k, ], lambda)
    sharpe_ratio(x_estimation[folds == k, ] %*% weights)
  }) |>
    mean(na.rm = TRUE)
}
ridge_lambda <- ridge_lambdas[which.max(map_dbl(ridge_lambdas, \(lambda) {
  cv_sharpe(ridge_weights, lambda)
}))]
ridge_sharpe <- c(
  estimation = sharpe_ratio(
    returns[estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda)
  ),
  test = sharpe_ratio(
    returns[!estimation, ] %*% ridge_weights(x_estimation, ridge_lambda)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-macro-predictors-r
#| include: false
# The macro predictors (Welch & Goyal) of month t - 1, known when month t
# starts, standardized with the estimation sample
macro_names <- c("dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar")
macro <- read_parquet("data/macro_predictors.parquet") |>
  transmute(date = date %m+% months(1), across(all_of(macro_names))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(macro_names), \(x) {
    (x - mean(x[date < test_start])) / sd(x[date < test_start])
  }))
```

```{python}
#| label: prepare-macro-predictors-py
#| include: false
#| eval: false
# The macro predictors (Welch & Goyal) of month t - 1, known when month t
# starts, standardized with the estimation sample
macro_names = ["dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar"]
in_estimation = pl.col("date") < test_start
macro = (
    pl.read_parquet("data/macro_predictors.parquet")
    .select(pl.col("date").dt.offset_by("1mo"), *macro_names)
    .with_columns(
        [
            (
                (pl.col(c) - pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).mean())
                / pl.col(c).filter(in_estimation).std()
            ).alias(c)
            for c in macro_names
        ]
    )
)
```

## Two uses of machine learning

- **Lectures 10 to 12:** estimate the SDF, the best portfolio of the zoo, directly. The SDF's weights are constant
- **The other use:** forecast each return, $E_t[r_{i,t+1}] = g(z_{i,t})$, with characteristics and the state of the economy in $z_{i,t}$. The function $g$ may be nonlinear and contain interactions
- A forecast is not yet a portfolio: we need a second step from forecasts to weights

::: {.highlight}
**Today:** machine learning forecasts of stock returns (Gu, Kelly & Xiu, 2020), regression trees and random forests on the zoo, and a portfolio from the forecasts. Does a flexible forecast of returns beat a well-shrunk SDF?
:::

# Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020)

## Empirical asset pricing via machine learning

- **Data:** almost 30,000 US stocks, March 1957 to December 2016, more than 6,200 a month on average. Our version from exercise 5, merged with CRSP: `r comma(characteristics_coverage$stocks)` stocks, `r format(characteristics_coverage$first, "%B %Y")` to `r format(characteristics_coverage$last, "%B %Y")`, about `r comma(characteristics_coverage$per_month, 100)` a month
- **Predictors:** 94 characteristics, each interacted with 8 macro predictors (Welch & Goyal), plus 74 industry dummies: $94 \times (8 + 1) + 74 = 920$
- **Samples:** training 1957–1974, validation 1975–1986, test 1987–2016. The models are refitted every year on a growing training sample; the validation sample rolls forward. Our trees and forests on the zoo are fitted once, as in lectures 10 to 12, and tested on `r year(test_start)`–`r year(sample_end)`
- **Methods:** OLS, partial least squares, principal component regression, elastic net, generalized linear models, random forests, gradient boosted trees, and neural networks with one to five layers

## Their forecasts

```{r}
nonlinear_r2 <- gkx_r2$r2[gkx_r2$group != "Linear"]
```

$$
R^2_{oos} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{(i,t) \in \text{test}} (r_{i,t+1} - \hat r_{i,t+1})^2}{\sum_{(i,t) \in \text{test}} r_{i,t+1}^2}
$$

- **Benchmark:** a forecast of zero, not the historical mean, which is too noisy for single stocks. OLS with all 920 predictors: `r number(gkx_r2$r2[1], 0.01)`%. OLS-3 with size, book-to-market and momentum only: `r number(gkx_r2$r2[2], 0.01)`%
- Trees and networks forecast best, `r number(min(nonlinear_r2), 0.01)` to `r number(max(nonlinear_r2), 0.01)`% a month. Small, but for stock returns a large number

## What predicts, and what it pays

- **The same few predictors** matter for all methods: price trends (short-term reversal, momentum, industry momentum), liquidity (market value, dollar volume, bid-ask spread) and volatility
- **Portfolios:** sort stocks each month into deciles of the forecast and buy the top, sell the bottom decile. Annualized out-of-sample Sharpe ratios of this long-short portfolio, with two ways to weight the stocks within a decile:

| Forecast | Value-weighted | Equal-weighted |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Four-layer network (NN4) | **1.35** | 2.45 |
| OLS-3 | 0.61 | 0.83 |

- **Equal weights** give small stocks as much weight as big ones: higher Sharpe ratios, but from stocks that are expensive to trade
- **Costs:** these portfolios turn over more than 100% of their value a month (their Table 8). Lecture 15 comes back to this

# Trees and forests

## Regression trees

::: {.box}
Split the sample in two, by one predictor and one threshold, so that the forecast errors fall most. Then split each half again
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\min_{j,\,s} \ \sum_{i:\, z_{ij} < s} (r_i - \bar r_{\text{left}})^2 + \sum_{i:\, z_{ij} \ge s} (r_i - \bar r_{\text{right}})^2
$$

- Each leaf forecasts the average return of its observations. Nonlinearities and interactions come for free: a split on momentum, then on last month's return
- **Depth** sets the complexity: deep trees fit the noise of the sample, and a small change in the data changes the whole tree
:::

## From a sort to a tree

```{r}
#| label: illustrate-tree
#| include: false
# One cross-section, as in the sort illustration of lecture 7: a tree of depth
# 2 on size and book-to-market, with at least 200 stocks in each leaf
illustration_depth <- 2
illustration_min_leaf <- 200
illustration_tree <- rpart(
  ret_excess ~ size + bm,
  data = cross_section,
  control = rpart.control(
    maxdepth = illustration_depth,
    minbucket = illustration_min_leaf,
    cp = 0
  )
)

# The 2 x 3 sort of lecture 8, with breakpoints from all stocks
sort_size_breaks <- c(0, 0.5, 1)
sort_bm_breaks <- c(0, 0.3, 0.7, 1)

# The rectangle of a node of the tree in the plane of size and book-to-market
split_rule <- function(node) {
  rule <- last(path.rpart(illustration_tree, node, print.it = FALSE)[[1]])
  parts <- regmatches(rule, regexec("^(\\w+)(<|>=)(.+)$", rule))[[1]]
  list(
    variable = parts[2],
    below = parts[3] == "<",
    value = as.numeric(parts[4])
  )
}
node_region <- function(node) {
  region <- c(size_low = 0, size_high = 1, bm_low = 0, bm_high = 1)
  ancestors <- node %/% 2^(seq_len(floor(log2(node))) - 1)
  for (k in rev(ancestors[ancestors > 1])) {
    rule <- split_rule(k)
    bound <- paste0(rule$variable, if (rule$below) "_high" else "_low")
    region[bound] <- rule$value
  }
  frame <- illustration_tree$frame[as.character(node), ]
  tibble(
    xmin = region[["bm_low"]],
    xmax = region[["bm_high"]],
    ymin = region[["size_low"]],
    ymax = region[["size_high"]],
    ret = frame$yval
  )
}

# The tree split by split: the regions after each step
tree_steps <- list(1, c(2, 3), c(4, 5, 3), c(4, 5, 6, 7))
sort_regions <- expand_grid(i = 1:2, j = 1:3) |>
  mutate(
    xmin = sort_bm_breaks[j],
    xmax = sort_bm_breaks[j + 1],
    ymin = sort_size_breaks[i],
    ymax = sort_size_breaks[i + 1]
  ) |>
  mutate(
    ret = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(k) {
      cross_section |>
        filter(
          between(bm, xmin[k], xmax[k]),
          between(size, ymin[k], ymax[k])
        ) |>
        pull(ret_excess) |>
        mean()
    })
  )

panel_names <- c(
  "Sort: breakpoints fixed in advance",
  "Tree: splits chosen by the returns"
)
# The inner edges of the regions: the breakpoints and the splits
inner_edges <- function(regions) {
  bind_rows(
    regions |> transmute(x = xmin, xend = xmin, y = ymin, yend = ymax),
    regions |> transmute(x = xmin, xend = xmax, y = ymin, yend = ymin)
  ) |>
    filter(x + xend > 0, y + yend > 0)
}
plot_step <- function(nodes) {
  tree_regions <- map(nodes, node_region) |> list_rbind()
  regions <- bind_rows(
    sort_regions |> mutate(panel = panel_names[1]),
    tree_regions |> mutate(panel = panel_names[2])
  ) |>
    mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_names))
  edges <- bind_rows(
    inner_edges(sort_regions) |> mutate(panel = panel_names[1]),
    inner_edges(tree_regions) |> mutate(panel = panel_names[2])
  ) |>
    mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_names))
  points <- expand_grid(
    cross_section,
    panel = factor(panel_names, levels = panel_names)
  )

  ggplot() +
    geom_point(
      data = points,
      aes(x = bm, y = size),
      color = grey,
      alpha = 0.2,
      size = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      data = edges,
      aes(
        x = x,
        xend = xend,
        y = y,
        yend = yend,
        color = panel,
        linetype = panel
      ),
      linewidth = 1.1
    ) +
    geom_label(
      data = regions,
      aes(
        x = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
        y = (ymin + ymax) / 2,
        label = percent(ret, 0.1),
        color = panel
      ),
      size = 4.2,
      linewidth = 0
    ) +
    # Dashed breakpoints as in lecture 7, the splits of the tree in red
    scale_color_manual(values = set_names(c(jet, ku_red), panel_names)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(
      values = set_names(c("dashed", "solid"), panel_names)
    ) +
    facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = sort_bm_breaks,
      labels = c("0", "30th", "70th", "100th")
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      breaks = sort_size_breaks,
      labels = c("0", "50th", "100th")
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(
      x = "Book-to-market (percentile in the month)",
      y = "Size (percentile in the month)"
    ) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      panel.border = element_rect(color = light, fill = NA),
      panel.spacing = unit(3, "lines"),
      # Room for the last axis label of the right panel
      plot.margin = margin(5.5, 20, 5.5, 5.5),
      strip.text = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0)
    )
}
# The text says that the first split is on size, with the bigger stocks in
# node 2, and gives the splits as percentiles
stopifnot(split_rule(2)$variable == "size", !split_rule(2)$below)
split_percentiles <- map(c(2, 4, 6), \(node) {
  ordinal(round(100 * split_rule(node)$value))
})
```

- `r format(illustration_month, "%B %Y")`, the month of lecture 7: `r comma(nrow(cross_section))` stocks of exercise 5. Labels: the average excess return in each region, equal-weighted
- **Sort:** the breakpoints of lecture 8, here from all stocks, whatever the returns

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- **Tree:** the first split, at the `r split_percentiles[[1]]` percentile of size, reduces the squared errors most. Then each half gets its own split on book-to-market: at the `r split_percentiles[[2]]` percentile among the bigger stocks, at the `r split_percentiles[[3]]` among the smaller ones
:::

## The zoo as a panel

```{r}
#| label: build-panel-r
#| include: false
# One row per anomaly and month: the return and the predictors known when the
# month starts. anomalies and macro: the hidden chunks at the top
momentum_months <- 12
panel <- anomalies |>
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "anomaly", values_to = "ret") |>
  mutate(ret = ret / 100) |>
  arrange(anomaly, date) |>
  mutate(
    ret_lag_1 = lag(ret),
    momentum_12 = slider::slide_dbl(
      lag(ret),
      mean,
      .before = momentum_months - 1,
      .complete = TRUE
    ),
    .by = anomaly
  ) |>
  left_join(macro, join_by(date)) |>
  drop_na()
```

```{python}
#| label: build-panel-py
#| include: false
#| eval: false
# One row per anomaly and month: the return and the predictors known when the
# month starts. anomalies and complete (the anomalies without gaps): lecture 10
momentum_months = 12
panel = (
    anomalies.select("date", *complete)
    .unpivot(index="date", variable_name="anomaly", value_name="ret")
    .with_columns(pl.col("ret") / 100)
    .sort("anomaly", "date")
    .with_columns(
        ret_lag_1=pl.col("ret").shift(1).over("anomaly"),
        momentum_12=pl.col("ret")
        .shift(1)
        .rolling_mean(momentum_months)
        .over("anomaly"),
    )
    .join(macro, on="date", how="left")
    .drop_nulls()
)
```

- **One row per anomaly and month,** like a panel of stocks: `r comma(nrow(panel))` rows of `r n_distinct(panel$anomaly)` anomalies, `r format(min(panel$date), "%B %Y")` to `r format(max(panel$date), "%B %Y")`
- **Target:** the return $r_{i,t+1}$ of the month. **Predictors,** known when the month starts: last month's return, factor momentum (the mean return of the last `r momentum_months` months) and `r length(macro_names)` macro predictors of the month before (Welch & Goyal), standardized with the estimation sample

```{r}
#| label: show-panel
#| echo: false
# Two anomalies in the last two months of the estimation sample
example_anomalies <- c(AssetGrowth = "Asset growth", BM = "Book-to-market")
panel |>
  filter(
    anomaly %in% names(example_anomalies),
    date >= test_start %m-% months(2),
    date < test_start
  ) |>
  arrange(anomaly, date) |>
  transmute(
    # A non-breaking space keeps month and year on one line
    Month = format(date, "%b\u00a0%Y"),
    Anomaly = example_anomalies[anomaly],
    Return = percent(ret, 0.1),
    last_month = percent(ret_lag_1, 0.1),
    momentum = percent(momentum_12, 0.1),
    across(all_of(macro_names), \(x) number(x, 0.01))
  ) |>
  # Two-line headers for the predictors. A plain HTML table lets the browser
  # size the columns to their content
  set_names(c(
    "Month",
    "Anomaly",
    "Return",
    "Last<br>month",
    "Factor<br>momentum",
    "Dividend-price<br>ratio",
    "T-bill<br>rate",
    "Term<br>spread",
    "Default<br>spread",
    "Stock<br>variance"
  )) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    escape = FALSE,
    align = "llrrrrrrrr",
    table.attr = 'data-quarto-disable-processing="true" style="width: 100%;"'
  )
```

## A tree on the zoo

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: fit-tree-r
# The sample split of lectures 10 to 12; the size of the tree
test_start <- ymd("2000-01-01")
tree_depth <- 2
min_leaf <- 500

train <- panel |> filter(date < test_start)
tree <- rpart(
  ret ~ momentum_12 + ret_lag_1,
  data = train,
  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = tree_depth, minbucket = min_leaf, cp = 0)
)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: fit-tree-py
#| eval: false
# The sample split of lectures 10 to 12; the size of the tree
test_start = date(2000, 1, 1)
tree_depth = 2
min_leaf = 500

train = panel.filter(pl.col("date") < test_start)
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=tree_depth, min_samples_leaf=min_leaf).fit(
    train.select("momentum_12", "ret_lag_1"), train["ret"]
)
```
:::

`train` holds the estimation sample. Each leaf keeps at least `r min_leaf` anomaly-months; `cp = 0` switches off an extra stopping rule of `rpart()` that scikit-learn does not have

## The leaves of the tree

```{r}
#| label: plot-tree
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
# The leaves of the tree as rectangles in the plane of its two predictors
frame <- tree$frame
splits <- tree$splits
leaf_bounds <- function(node) {
  bounds <- list(momentum_12 = c(-Inf, Inf), ret_lag_1 = c(-Inf, Inf))
  path <- path.rpart(tree, node, print.it = FALSE)[[1]][-1]
  for (rule in path) {
    parts <- regmatches(rule, regexec("^(\\w+)(<|>=)(.+)$", rule))[[1]]
    value <- as.numeric(parts[4])
    if (parts[3] == "<") {
      bounds[[parts[2]]][2] <- value
    } else {
      bounds[[parts[2]]][1] <- value
    }
  }
  bounds
}
leaves <- as.numeric(rownames(frame)[frame$var == "<leaf>"])
range_m <- quantile(train$momentum_12, c(0.005, 0.995))
range_r <- quantile(train$ret_lag_1, c(0.005, 0.995))
leaf_data <- map(leaves, \(node) {
  b <- leaf_bounds(node)
  tibble(
    xmin = max(b$momentum_12[1], range_m[1]),
    xmax = min(b$momentum_12[2], range_m[2]),
    ymin = max(b$ret_lag_1[1], range_r[1]),
    ymax = min(b$ret_lag_1[2], range_r[2]),
    forecast = frame$yval[rownames(frame) == node],
    n = frame$n[rownames(frame) == node]
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

ggplot(leaf_data) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = forecast),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
      y = (ymin + ymax) / 2,
      label = paste0(number(forecast * 100, 0.01), "%\na month"),
      color = rescale(forecast) < 0.25
    ),
    size = 4.5,
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  # Dark text on the light leaf, white text on the dark ones
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = jet, "FALSE" = "white"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#b3b3b3", high = ku_red, labels = percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    x = paste(
      "Average monthly return over the last",
      momentum_months,
      "months (factor momentum)"
    ),
    y = "Last month's return",
    fill = "Forecast"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

- Each rectangle is a leaf, with its forecast: the average return of its anomaly-months in the estimation sample
- The first split is on factor momentum: anomalies that did well over the last year keep doing well (Ehsani & Linnainmaa, 2022). Among them, last month's winners earn most

## Random forests

- **Bagging:** grow many deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the data, and average their forecasts. Averaging removes much of the variance of single trees
- **Random predictors:** at each split, a tree may use only a random subset of `mtry` predictors. The trees differ more, so their average gains more
- **Tuning parameters:** the number of predictors per split (`mtry`) and the smallest node that may still be split (`min_n`). Choose them by cross-validation on consecutive blocks of time, as in lecture 11

## Tuning a forest in R and Python

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: tune-forest-r
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(train)
n_folds <- 5
n_trees <- 100
forest_grid <- expand_grid(mtry = c(1, 3, 7), min_n = c(500, 2000))

# Consecutive blocks of months as folds, as in lecture 11
block_folds <- train |>
  mutate(block = ceiling(dense_rank(date) / (n_distinct(date) / n_folds))) |>
  group_vfold_cv(group = block, v = n_folds)
forest_model <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = n_trees) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 2027) |>
  set_mode("regression")
forest_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_formula(ret ~ ret_lag_1 + momentum_12 + dp + tbl + tms + dfy + svar) |>
  add_model(forest_model)
forest_tuning <- tune_grid(forest_workflow, block_folds, grid = forest_grid)
forest_fit <- forest_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(select_best(forest_tuning, metric = "rmse")) |>
  fit(train)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: tune-forest-py
#| eval: false
n_folds = 5
n_trees = 100
forest_grid = {"max_features": [1, 3, 7], "min_samples_split": [500, 2000]}
predictors = ["ret_lag_1", "momentum_12", "dp", "tbl", "tms", "dfy", "svar"]

# Consecutive blocks of months as folds, as in lecture 11
months = train["date"].rank("dense")
blocks = np.ceil(months / (months.max() / n_folds)).to_numpy()
forest_model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=n_trees, random_state=2027, n_jobs=-1)
search = GridSearchCV(
    forest_model,
    forest_grid,
    cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=n_folds),
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
)
search.fit(train.select(predictors), train["ret"], groups=blocks)
```
:::

`ranger` and scikit-learn draw different random trees, so their forecasts differ a little

# From forecasts to a portfolio

## Forecasts as expected returns

```{r}
#| label: forecast-portfolios
#| include: false
test_rows <- panel$date >= test_start
best_forest <- select_best(forest_tuning, metric = "rmse")
# OLS on the same predictors as the forest
forecast_formula <- extract_preprocessor(forest_workflow)
n_predictors <- length(all.vars(forecast_formula)) - 1
forecasts <- list(
  predict(lm(forecast_formula, data = train), panel),
  predict(tree, panel),
  predict(forest_fit, panel)$.pred
) |>
  set_names(c("OLS", paste("Tree of depth", tree_depth), "Random forest"))

# Each month: the mean-variance weights with the forecasts as expected
# returns, the covariance matrix of the estimation sample and the ridge
# penalty of lecture 11
covariance <- cov(x_estimation)
forecast_row <- function(method, forecast) {
  oos_r2 <- 1 -
    sum((panel$ret[test_rows] - forecast[test_rows])^2) /
      sum(panel$ret[test_rows]^2)
  portfolio <- panel |>
    mutate(forecast = forecast) |>
    select(date, anomaly, forecast, ret) |>
    nest(data = -date) |>
    mutate(
      ret = map_dbl(data, \(d) {
        order <- match(colnames(returns), d$anomaly)
        weights <- solve(
          covariance + ridge_lambda * diag(ncol(returns)),
          d$forecast[order]
        )
        sum(weights * d$ret[order])
      })
    )
  tibble(
    method = method,
    oos_r2 = oos_r2,
    estimation = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date < test_start]),
    test = sharpe_ratio(portfolio$ret[portfolio$date >= test_start])
  )
}
forecast_rows <- imap(forecasts, \(forecast, method) {
  forecast_row(method, forecast)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# The samples in the tables: the forecasts start after the first year
forecast_start <- year(min(panel$date))
forecast_years <- paste0(forecast_start, "–", year(test_start) - 1)
test_years <- paste0(year(test_start), "–", year(sample_end))
```

$$
\omega_t = (\hat\Sigma + \lambda I)^{-1}\,\hat\mu_t \qquad \hat\mu_t: \text{the forecasts for all anomalies in month } t
$$

```{r}
#| label: forecast-table
#| echo: false
forecast_rows |>
  transmute(
    Forecast = method,
    `Out-of-sample R²` = percent(oos_r2, 0.01),
    "Sharpe ratio {forecast_years}" := number(estimation, 0.01),
    "Sharpe ratio {test_years}" := number(test, 0.01)
  )
```

- The covariance matrix and the penalty are those of the ridge SDF of lecture 11 (Sharpe ratio `r number(ridge_sharpe[["test"]], 0.01)` in the test sample); only the expected returns change every month
- The tuned forest uses `r best_forest$mtry` of the `r n_predictors` predictors per split and splits only nodes with at least `r best_forest$min_n` anomaly-months. No forecast portfolio comes near the static ridge SDF

## Trees for the SDF

- **Bryzgalova, Pelger & Zhu (2025)** use trees to build portfolios, not to forecast. Split the stocks at the median of one characteristic, then each half at the median of the same or another one, up to four times: conditional sorts, such as size, then book-to-market, then size again
- **Every node** of the trees, final or intermediate, is a value-weighted, long-only portfolio. The splits stay at the medians; the data decide which nodes to keep
- **Pruning:** keep the few nodes that together span the SDF best. Their SDF extends the shrunk SDF of Kozak, Nagel & Santosh (2020) from lecture 11: mean-variance weights with lasso and ridge penalties and shrunk means, tuned on a validation sample
- **Their result:** compared with combinations of dozens of single and double sorts, and with portfolios sorted on machine learning forecasts, their few portfolios have up to three times higher out-of-sample Sharpe ratios and alphas

::: {.highlight}
Trees can also serve the SDF of lectures 10 to 12: the trees propose the portfolios, the shrunk SDF picks and weights them
:::

## Scoreboard

```{r}
#| label: scoreboard
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Portfolio = c(
    "Ridge (prior on Sharpe ratios)",
    paste("Forecasts:", forecast_rows$method)
  ),
  Inputs = c(
    paste(ncol(returns), "anomalies"),
    # The tree of depth 2 splits on two predictors only
    paste(
      c(n_predictors, length(attr(tree$terms, "term.labels")), n_predictors),
      "predictors"
    )
  ),
  estimation = c(ridge_sharpe[["estimation"]], forecast_rows$estimation),
  test = c(ridge_sharpe[["test"]], forecast_rows$test)
) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimation, test), \(x) number(x, 0.01))) |>
  rename(
    `Sharpe ratio, estimation` = estimation,
    "Sharpe ratio {test_years}" := test
  )
```

- Forecasts need `r momentum_months` months of history, so their estimation sample starts in `r forecast_start`; the rows of lectures 10 to 12 stay on the scoreboard
- **Lecture 14:** a neural network for the forecasts, and a network that learns the SDF directly
